name: Murphy's Law
statement: Anything that can go wrong will go wrong.
meaning: If there is a way for something to fail, then eventually — often at the worst possible moment — it will.
mechanism: Over enough trials, every possible failure mode gets its chance: a low-probability fault becomes nearly certain if the system runs long enough or often enough. Read as engineering rather than gloom, the 'law' is a design stance — assume the unlikely failure will occur, and build so it cannot, or so it fails safely when it does.
example: A part can be fitted two ways and only one is correct. Murphy's Law says that on some assembly, someone will fit it the wrong way — so the real fix is to make the wrong way physically impossible.
whyItMatters: As discipline rather than fatalism it drives defensive design: foolproofing, redundancy, and testing for the failure you are sure won't happen. Designing as though Murphy is right is how you keep him wrong.
misreadings: It is not a claim that the universe is malicious or that everything always fails — it is a prompt to take low-probability failures seriously, not a prediction that they are certain on any single run. Treated as gloom it is useless; treated as a design checklist it is invaluable.
origin: Attributed to the aerospace engineer Edward A. Murphy Jr. around 1949, during rocket-sled deceleration tests (project MX981) at what became Edwards Air Force Base, and popularised by the project's lead, Colonel John Stapp, at a press conference.

sources.text: Spark, N. T. (2006). A History of Murphy's Law.
